title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Water-utility attacks now hit at least 12 states — sources tie the campaign to Iran as operators fall back to manual control
items.content_text: The coordinated campaign against internet-facing water and wastewater PLCs is still developing. As of 10 August, SecurityWeek reports New Jersey and Alabama have joined the confirmed list — Cape May and Woodbine, NJ (phone systems disrupted) and Childersburg, AL (ICS targeted, water service unaffected) — after intrusions across at least a dozen states. Minnesota was first, confirming 30-plus systems (26–27 July); Michigan (nine systems, 1 Aug), South Dakota and Georgia followed, where Clayton County Water Authority (serving ~300,000) issued a boil-water advisory. Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Washington have warned utilities without confirming hits; New York added $9M in grants. Attackers changed device IPs and passwords to lock operators out and forced Braham and others onto manual control, though officials stress drinking water stayed safe. US intelligence assesses Iran the likely actor; attribution stays officially unconfirmed and disputed.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: FBI/EPA alert & MNIT / Michigan / Clayton County (GA) / city statements (Braham, South St. Paul, Plymouth, Maple Plain); Tenable assessment — via CBS News, Bloomberg, ABC News, Axios, SecurityWeek, The Register, The Hacker News, NBC News, CNN, Washington Post & MPR
_otthreatfeed.date_note: 26–27 Jul incident — MN confirmed 28 Jul; FBI/EPA 7 states 30–31 Jul; Michigan 1 Aug; NJ & Alabama confirmed 10 Aug (SecurityWeek); at least 12 states; Iran-likely, still developing

items.title: Cyberattack knocks North Carolina’s three ports onto manual gate processing
items.content_text: The North Carolina State Ports Authority confirmed it detected a cyberattack on 4 August that triggered a systems-wide IT outage across the Port of Wilmington, the Port of Morehead City and the Charlotte Inland Port. Terminals stayed open, but gate operations fell back to manual processing, slowing truck turn times and cargo flow — Wilmington alone averages roughly 5,000 container gate moves a week, and the two seaports together handle about 4.4 million short tons a year. The authority says it contained the intrusion the same day, activated its cyber contingency plan on 5 August and had operations trending back toward normal by 7 August, with no evidence so far that sensitive data was taken. No actor has claimed it and no ransomware family has been named. For OT and logistics defenders it is another clean example of a business-systems outage throttling physical throughput without a control system being touched.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: North Carolina State Ports Authority statement — via BleepingComputer, The Maritime Executive & WECT
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Detected 4 Aug — recovery under way, operations easing back to normal by 7 Aug 2026

items.title: Coca-Cola confirms Fairlife data was stolen as production restarts after ransomware stop
items.content_text: Coca-Cola said on 27 July that its Fairlife dairy subsidiary has resumed the majority of production at all four of its US plants, roughly ten days after a ransomware event forced a full production suspension first disclosed in a 16 July SEC 8-K. The company says retail availability was largely cushioned by existing inventory and that product quality and safety were never affected. The extortion side then escalated: the Anubis ransomware group had listed Coca-Cola/Fairlife on its leak site on 20 July, claiming about 1 TB of stolen data and encryption of Nutanix infrastructure, and on 28 July Coca-Cola confirmed that data was in fact taken in the attack after its 27 July ransom deadline lapsed. For OT defenders the lesson stands even as lines restart: ransomware in the plant IT and production-scheduling layer can halt a food & beverage operation without ever touching a controller.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Coca-Cola statement & press release / SEC 8-K / Anubis leak-site claim — via Just Food, Reuters & SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 16 Jul — production resumed 27 Jul, data theft confirmed 28 Jul 2026

items.title: Cisco ASA/FTD SSL-VPN zero-day exploited to crash firewalls — the perimeter box fronting many OT remote-access paths
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20349 on 11 August, an actively-exploited flaw in the Remote Access SSL VPN service of Cisco Secure Firewall ASA and FTD software. Because of inadequate error checking on HTTP requests, an unauthenticated remote attacker can send a crafted request that forces an unexpected device reload — no credentials or user interaction, low complexity, availability impact only. Cisco confirmed exploitation in the wild, and CISA added the bug to its KEV catalog the same day with a 14 August federal remediation deadline; Cisco says no workaround fully addresses it. ASA/FTD firewalls segment and front many OT and remote-site networks, so a crash-loop here can knock out remote access, monitoring and secure connectivity into a plant — a denial-of-availability against the very device meant to protect it. It lands amid an intensifying run on edge and remote-access appliances (see the SonicWall, VeloCloud and Cisco FMC items above).

items.title: SonicWall SMA 1000 flaws now weaponized by ransomware crews — a favorite OT remote-access on-ramp under active attack
items.content_text: The SMA 1000 zero-days have escalated from targeted intrusions to broad ransomware use. Around 10 August CISA, BleepingComputer and The Hacker News reported that the two flaws — CVE-2026-15409, a maximum-severity (CVSS 10) unauthenticated server-side request forgery, and CVE-2026-15410 (CVSS 7.2), a post-auth OS command-injection — are now being chained to root by ransomware operators, with INC Ransomware the dominant actor and Resecurity noting it has accelerated since early August. The original activity, tied by Volexity to cluster UTA0533 and by Rapid7 MDR to stealthy credential, session-database and TOTP MFA-seed theft, dates to SonicWall’s 14 July disclosure; CISA KEV-listed both with a 17 July federal deadline. SMA-class VPN/remote-access gateways commonly bridge into OT networks, so stolen sessions and MFA seeds are exactly the on-ramp defenders keep seeing.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 14 Jul 2026 — ransomware exploitation confirmed ~10 Aug 2026

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator CVSS 10 zero-day exploited — SD-WAN control plane for remote and plant sites under attack
items.content_text: Arista and CISA confirmed active in-the-wild exploitation of CVE-2026-16812, a maximum-severity (CVSS 10.0) unauthenticated OS command-injection flaw in on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO), the centralized platform used to configure and manage VeloCloud SD-WAN fabrics and their edge appliances. A remote attacker needs no credentials to reach privileged internal functions and run arbitrary commands on the orchestrator host — and Arista warns that compromising the VCO can extend attacker access to the managed VeloCloud Edge devices themselves. CISA added the flaw to its KEV catalog on 27 July with a 30 July federal remediation deadline. SD-WAN orchestrators frequently stitch together remote sites, substations and plant networks, so a compromised control plane is a direct route into the WAN paths that reach OT.

items.title: Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center hard-coded-password zero-day exploited — the box that controls plant-perimeter firewalls
items.content_text: Cisco disclosed CVE-2026-20316 on 29 July, a hard-coded-password flaw in Cisco Secure Firewall Management Center (FMC) that lets an unauthenticated attacker, on the network or the internet, log in to an affected instance with a low-privilege account and no valid credentials. The base CVSS is only 5.3, but Cisco assigned it a High security-impact rating because it can be chained to escalate privileges, and Cisco PSIRT confirmed it was exploited as a zero-day before a fix existed. CISA added it to the KEV catalog the same day. FMC is the central management plane for Cisco Secure Firewall deployments, including the firewalls that segment and front many OT networks — so a foothold here lets an attacker read the ruleset, weaken segmentation or map the environment before touching a controller.

items.title: Cl0p launches a large-scale extortion wave against PTC Windchill and FlexPLM — a manufacturing PLM backbone under active data theft
items.content_text: The Cl0p ransomware crew is running a broad data-theft campaign against internet-exposed PTC Windchill and FlexPLM servers, exploiting the critical (CVSS 9.8) unauthenticated remote-code-execution flaw CVE-2026-12569 — already in CISA’s KEV catalog — to drop JSP web shells and exfiltrate engineering data. Researchers at BleepingComputer and The Hacker News report Cl0p began mass extortion around 20 July, emailing large internal distribution lists with a “Windchill PDMLink module serious data leak” subject to pressure victims, with confirmed impact in manufacturing, automotive, aerospace and apparel. Windchill sits deep in engineering environments — holding CAD, BOM and process data and often bridging enterprise and plant networks — so a web shell here is a foothold with a clear line toward OT-adjacent assets. Cl0p has a long record of turning a single PLM/file-transfer flaw into a mass campaign, and this one is now moving fast.

items.title: Progress LoadMaster command-injection flaw added to CISA KEV — another edge appliance fronting OT under active attack
items.content_text: On 7 August CISA added CVE-2026-8037, an OS command-injection flaw in Progress’ LoadMaster application-delivery controller / load balancer, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog after confirming exploitation in the wild. LoadMaster appliances commonly sit in front of application and remote-access traffic, terminating and steering sessions into internal networks — so command execution on one hands an attacker a privileged position on the on-ramp, not just a single service. It lands squarely in the edge/management-appliance wave defenders have been fighting all month (N-able N-central, Cisco ASA/FTD and FMC, Arista VeloCloud, SonicWall SMA 1000), the same class of box that quietly bridges corporate and plant networks. For OT owners the pattern is now routine: the internet-facing appliance is compromised long before any PLC is touched.

items.title: CERT.PL details a second Sandworm sabotage of Poland’s grid — a novel private-APN pivot from a wind farm into a CHP plant’s PLCs
items.content_text: Poland’s CERT.PL published a follow-up report over the weekend on a second, previously undisclosed December 2025 attack on the country’s energy sector, run in parallel with the known Russia-linked Sandworm strike and described as “purely destructive.” It hit a small combined-heat-and-power plant supplying heat to about 50,000 residents. Attackers entered through an internet-exposed Fortinet VPN/firewall at a wind farm, pivoted to a Teltonika cellular router, and tunnelled over SSH into a private APN network the distribution operator uses to reach substation ICS — what CERT.PL calls the first known use of a private APN as an attack vector. From there they reached a Wago PLC, then Siemens PLCs they switched to “stop” and password-locked, shutting a steam turbine and water-treatment system; Moxa serial servers/switches and ABB/Schneider drives were also targeted. Operators restored service from backups, but several ICS devices were deliberately bricked.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CERT.PL Energy Sector Incident Follow-up Report — via SecurityWeek
_otthreatfeed.date_note: Attack Dec 2025 — CERT.PL report disclosed 8 Aug, reported 10 Aug 2026

items.title: World Leaks dumps Reliance files tied to India’s largest nuclear plant
items.content_text: The extortion group World Leaks posted a large cache of files on its dark-web site that it attributed to India’s Reliance Group, including purported blueprints and supplier details connected to the Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant. Reliance — a contractor building infrastructure for Kudankulam Units 3 and 4 — confirmed a “partial breach” of data held on a server run by third-party data-center provider Yotta and said it had informed the government. The roughly 19,000 most sensitive files reportedly include ventilation and cooling-system drawings and a control-room floor layout, but not the Russian-supplied reactor core systems. This is a supply-chain data exposure rather than an OT compromise — but leaked engineering detail on a nuclear site shows how contractor and third-party data becomes an OT risk of its own.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Reliance Group / Reuters — via Business Standard & Al Jazeera

items.title: Blackfield ransomware demands $2M from motor maker Nidec after breaching a Taiwanese subsidiary
items.content_text: The Blackfield ransomware crew has listed Nidec — the large Japanese electric-motor and industrial-component manufacturer — on its leak site, demanding $2 million and claiming it stole more than two terabytes of data from subsidiary Nidec Chaun-Choung Technology in Taiwan. The group says the archive spans employee, financial, procurement, manufacturing, legal and IT records, and is offering to sell or publish it if unpaid. Nidec states the subsidiary runs on an independent network that limited the intrusion’s reach and has not confirmed the volume or contents of any stolen files — the figures come from the attacker, which has every incentive to inflate them. No production impact has been reported, but it is another reminder that manufacturing remains the most-targeted sector for industrial ransomware.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Blackfield leak-site claim / Nidec — via BleepingComputer

items.title: Swiss train maker Stadler Rail refuses $12.3M ransom after a supplier data-exchange breach
items.content_text: Stadler Rail confirmed the Everest extortion group stole technical data after compromising credentials for a data-exchange platform the manufacturer shares with one of its suppliers. Stadler says its own IT systems, production lines and in-service rail vehicles worldwide were not affected, that the stolen files are technical material with no bearing on railway safety, and that it will not pay — publicly stating it is “not susceptible to extortion” and filing a criminal complaint with Thurgau police. Everest, a group that shifted from encryption to pure data-theft extortion, is demanding roughly $12.3 million (CHF 10 million). For OT defenders in transit and manufacturing this is the recurring supply-chain pattern: the breach landed on a shared third-party platform, not the target’s plant, yet exposed sensitive engineering data all the same.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Stadler Rail statement / Everest leak-site claim — via BleepingComputer, The Register & Railway Gazette

items.title: Cyberattack halts eight Ceva Logistics warehouses in Europe — a warehousing/fulfillment disruption rippling into retail supply chains
items.content_text: Freight and contract-logistics giant Ceva Logistics confirmed a cyberattack that disrupted operations at eight of its European warehouses between roughly 29 July and 1 August, delaying shipments for numerous retail customers whose inventory sits in those sites. Ceva says its air, ocean, ground and rail transportation operations kept running normally — only the contract-logistics (warehousing/fulfillment) arm was hit. Coverage from The Record, TechCrunch and The Register (10–11 August) reports exposed personal data — names, addresses, phone numbers, emails and order details, but not payment or credential data — with downstream impact on customers including Dutch e-commerce firm Bol, De Bijenkorf, Ace & Tate and Valve’s Steam hardware business in Europe. Dutch and other authorities are investigating. For OT and logistics defenders it is a reminder that warehouse-management and fulfillment systems are production systems too: an IT-layer intrusion can stop physical goods moving without ever touching a conveyor or PLC.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Ceva Logistics statement / Dutch DPA — via The Record, TechCrunch, The Register & FreightWaves

items.title: CISA re-issues Iranian PLC-attack advisory (AA26-097A) — CyberAv3ngers now confirmed hitting Rockwell, Schneider and Siemens controllers
items.content_text: CISA, FBI, NSA, EPA, DOE and Cyber Command updated advisory AA26-097A on 22 July, broadening the campaign that Iran’s IRGC-linked CyberAv3ngers persona has run against internet-exposed programmable logic controllers across US critical infrastructure. The update documents project-file exfiltration for the first time, adds detection guidance for malicious changes to reusable code modules inside Rockwell Automation PLC programs, and expands confirmed targeting to Schneider Electric and Siemens controllers — with actors abusing the vendors’ own engineering software (Studio 5000, EcoStruxure Control Expert, TIA Portal) to reach exposed PLCs. Agencies say victims in water/wastewater, energy and government have already suffered operational disruption and financial loss after actors manipulated PLC logic and altered HMI/SCADA readings. This is the agency-level framing behind this week’s Minnesota water incident (see top story): confirmed hands-on manipulation of control logic, not reconnaissance, spanning multiple sectors and controller vendors.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA AA26-097A (updated 22 Jul 2026) / FBI / NSA / EPA / DOE / USCYBERCOM — via CISA & Industrial Cyber

items.title: Dragos Q2 2026: industrial ransomware climbs to 1,140 incidents — and rarely needs to touch a PLC to stop production
items.content_text: Dragos’ Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis (published 11 August) counts 1,140 ransomware incidents affecting industrial organisations for the quarter, up about 12% from 1,020 in Q1. Manufacturing again absorbed the bulk — roughly 747 incidents, about 65% of the total — with discrete and process makers hit hardest. The report’s operational point is the one OT defenders should internalise: attackers almost never gain ICS-native control, yet they still cause downtime, precautionary shutdowns, loss of view and safety pressure by crippling the IT systems plants depend on. The recurring access paths are unchanged — stolen credentials, compromised remote access, and weak IT/OT segmentation — which is why the fix set is architectural, not signature-based.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Q2 2026 Industrial Ransomware Analysis — via Help Net Security

items.title: Forescout: 4,400+ Rockwell controllers still sit on the open internet — 22 in the cities just hit
items.content_text: As the water-utility campaign kept spreading, Forescout’s Vedere Labs published a scan (6 August) that quantifies the exposure attackers are walking through. A 3 August Shodan query found 4,407 devices answering on port 44818 — the EtherNet/IP service built into Rockwell Automation/Allen-Bradley PLCs — with about 65% in the US, 12% in Canada and 3% in Spain. Crucially, more than 70% of the US-based controllers sit on large mobile-carrier networks, reached through cellular routers rather than enterprise circuits, which is exactly how many small water systems connect remote sites and why they slip past IT asset management. Researchers matched 22 exposed PLCs to cities named in the recent attacks, and roughly 86% of the hosts in those cities ran firmware susceptible to the long-standing CVE-2017-16740. The finding lands the same week CISA and the FBI again told operators to get controllers off the public internet — and shows how many still are not.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Forescout Vedere Labs research — via CyberScoop, The Hacker News & Industrial Cyber

items.title: Unit 42 chains three Siemens ROX II zero-days to root on industrial switches
items.content_text: Palo Alto Networks’ Unit 42 disclosed a three-vulnerability exploit chain in Siemens ROX II operating-system switches — ruggedized devices used to route traffic inside substation, rail and plant networks. Chained together (CVE-2025-40948, -40947 and -40949, the last rated CVSS 9.1), an attacker moves from arbitrary file disclosure through a feature-key privilege-escalation flaw to full, persistent root access on the device. Individually the bugs range from medium to critical; the value of the write-up is showing how ordinary configuration and logic weaknesses compose into device takeover, and how a compromised OT switch becomes a durable pivot for lateral movement across the very network it segments. Siemens has published advisories (SSA-973901, -078743, -081142) and fixes in ROX II firmware V2.17.1.

items.title: An AI agent is now doing the exploiting — CISA adds Tomcat, Langflow and N-central flaws tied to autonomous attacks
items.content_text: CISA added three actively-exploited flaws to KEV on 4 August, and the notable thread is who — or what — is behind one of them. Researchers attribute exploitation of an Apache Tomcat cluster-encryption bypass (CVE-2026-34486, CVSS 7.5) to an AI-enabled autonomous campaign run by a China-based actor tracked as knaithe / KnYuan, reportedly driving the DeepSeek model through a “Hermes Agent” framework to scan for and exploit internet-exposed devices at machine speed. The same batch adds a Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-9198, CVSS 9.8) in the popular AI app-builder and a second N-able N-central authentication bypass (CVE-2026-18556) after confirmed on-prem server takeovers. None are OT products, but all are exactly the internet-facing IT and dev-tooling that fronts or bridges into plant networks — and agent-driven exploitation compresses the patch-to-attack window OT teams already struggle to meet.

items.title: CISA’s 13 August ICS batch adds a further 14 advisories across Siemens, Schneider and medical devices
items.content_text: Two days after ICS Patch Tuesday, CISA published a second large batch on 13 August — the ICSA-26-225 series plus ICSMA-26-225-01. Named entries include Siemens License Server (ICSA-26-225-07), where multiple flaws can allow privilege escalation and arbitrary file reads on the licensing host that a great many Siemens engineering tools depend on, and Siemens Parasolid V38.1 (ICSA-26-225-10), an out-of-bounds read in the geometric-modelling component that a malicious model file can trigger to execute code in the context of the current process. Schneider Electric’s PowerChute Serial Shutdown also features, alongside a medical-device advisory. Nothing in the batch is reported as exploited in the wild. Treat it as scheduled patch-and-monitor work, with priority on anything reachable from an engineering workstation or a shared licence server — those hosts sit close to project files and controller programming paths.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS advisories (ICSA-26-225 series, ICSMA-26-225-01) / Siemens ProductCERT / Schneider Electric

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: a max-severity Siemens SIMATIC IoT2050 auth flaw headlines the month’s fixes
items.content_text: Siemens, Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact shipped their August advisories on 11 August, and the volume matters as much as any single flaw. Siemens published around ten new advisories, led by a maximum-severity (CVSS 10) missing-authentication issue in SIMATIC IoT2050 Advanced gateways that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker run arbitrary code with elevated privileges, plus a critical code-execution flaw in Siveillance Video management servers. High-severity fixes touch Solid Edge, Simcenter Nastran and Femap, Parasolid, the Siemens License Server and Logo! Soft Comfort — issues that can crash apps, run code, escalate privileges or leak files. Schneider Electric and Phoenix Contact added their own advisories. None are reported exploited yet — but this gear sits at the core of energy, water and manufacturing plants, and the patch-to-exploit window keeps shrinking.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Siemens ProductCERT / Schneider Electric / Phoenix Contact PSIRT — via SecurityWeek

items.title: CISA’s 11 August advisories: Mitsubishi Electric FA engineering software and Iconics, plus Delta, GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy
items.content_text: The same day as August Patch Tuesday, CISA issued its own batch of ICS advisories (the ICSA-26-223 series) spanning several major OT vendors. The headline entries update Mitsubishi Electric guidance on authentication-bypass weaknesses across multiple FA (factory-automation) engineering-software products, and flag issues in Mitsubishi’s Iconics Digital Solutions SCADA/visualization suite. The batch also covers Delta Electronics engineering tools — including CNCSoft-G2 and the COMMGR simulation utility — alongside advisories touching GE Vernova and Hitachi Energy grid products. None are reported as exploited, but FA engineering software and SCADA visualization sit right at the programming and supervisory layer of plants and substations, so a cross-check against inventory is worth the time.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICS Advisories (ICSA-26-223 series) / Mitsubishi Electric / Delta Electronics / GE Vernova / Hitachi Energy — via Industrial Cyber

items.title: Siemens SICAM 8 grid-automation devices — DoS flaws and insecure OPC UA defaults
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-197-05 covers multiple vulnerabilities across Siemens SICAM 8 products, including SICAM A8000 and EGS device firmware used in substation automation and RTU roles. An HTTP-accessible debugging interface can let an authenticated attacker crash the web process for a denial-of-service condition (CVE-2026-54798 through -54801), and the affected application ships with a default configuration that disables all OPC UA security mechanisms — leaving that channel open to unauthorized access and control unless hardened. The advisory flags impact to the Energy and Critical Manufacturing sectors; Siemens directs customers to firmware V26.20 / V26.20.0 or later.

items.title: Rockwell Logix controllers — CVSS 9.2 flaws force an unrecoverable fault, in CISA’s 16 July batch
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-197-06 covers denial-of-service flaws in Rockwell Automation CompactLogix, ControlLogix, Compact GuardLogix and GuardLogix controllers, with CISA assigning a CVSS 9.2 base score to the most severe entries (CVE-2025-12012 and CVE-2025-11698): an unauthenticated, low-complexity network attacker can write invalid file data and drive a controller into a major non-recoverable fault (MNRF) that requires on-site personnel to physically recover the device. A companion advisory (ICSA-26-197-08) flags a DoS issue in the Flex 5000 adapter. Rockwell began pushing firmware on 14 July. These are workhorse controllers on discrete and process floors, so an availability hit that halts a line or batch is a real operational event even without code execution.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-197-06 & -08 / Rockwell PSIRT

items.title: CISA’s 23 July batch: Panduit IntraVUE lets an IT-side attacker reach control devices, plus Rockwell ThinManager, Weintek and Johnson Controls
items.content_text: CISA published seven fresh ICS advisories on 23 July (the ICSA-26-204 series) covering MZ Automation, Rockwell Automation, Panduit, Weintek and Johnson Controls — none known to be exploited, but several worth a scan. Panduit IntraVUE (ICSA-26-204-04, versions ≤3.2.1a14) stores passwords in plaintext, and CISA warns an attacker with IT-network access could manipulate connected industrial devices without physical access — exactly the IT-to-OT pivot defenders worry about. Weintek’s cMT3092X HMI (ICSA-26-204-03) lets a non-privileged user escalate rights or read other users’ credentials, and the batch adds Rockwell ThinManager (a widely deployed thin-client management server) and two Johnson Controls Metasys building-automation advisories. Small, IT-adjacent OT devices like these rarely make the asset inventory.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA ICSA-26-204-03 / -04 / -05 — via CISA & Patrick Coyle (Chemical Facility Security News)

items.title: CISA’s 28 July batch: Siemens SIMATIC S7-PLCSIM Advanced and Desigo CC among the ICSA-26-209 advisories
items.content_text: CISA published a fresh set of ICS advisories on 28 July (the ICSA-26-209 series). Two Siemens entries stand out: SIMATIC S7-PLCSIM Advanced (ICSA-26-209-03), where mishandling of high-volume multicast traffic can exhaust memory and let an unauthenticated attacker on the local network segment force a denial-of-service condition, and the Desigo CC building-management family (ICSA-26-209-01, versions V7, V8 and V9), affected by an OpenSSL stack-based buffer overflow that could cause a DoS or potentially remote code execution. The batch lands alongside a separate Rockwell Automation FactoryTalk Services Platform advisory (ICSA-26-202-07). None are reported as exploited, but PLC-simulation, building-management and FactoryTalk platform software sit close to engineering and plant operations, so they warrant an inventory cross-check.

items.title: CISA’s 30 July batch: eleven ICSA-26-211 advisories span Rockwell Logix comms modules, Siemens SIMATIC, Schneider IGSS and the MZ Automation IEC 60870 stack
items.content_text: CISA published eleven ICS advisories on 30 July (the ICSA-26-211 series). Among them, ICSA-26-211-05 covers a denial-of-service flaw in Rockwell Automation CompactLogix 5380, ControlLogix 5580 and the 1756-EN4TR communications module, where crafted traffic can knock the controller or adapter offline. ICSA-26-211-04 republishes Schneider Electric’s IGSS SCADA advisory, and other entries mirror Siemens SIMATIC ProductCERT notes and a vulnerability in MZ Automation’s lib60870 — an open-source IEC 60870-5 telecontrol library embedded in many utility RTU and gateway products. None are reported as exploited, but the comms-module and telecontrol-library items sit directly on grid and plant communication paths, so they warrant an inventory cross-check.

items.title: CISA’s 6 August advisories: ABB Ability Zenon SCADA/HMI and Johnson Controls TL280
items.content_text: CISA published fresh ICS advisories on 6 August (the ICSA-26-218 series). ICSA-26-218-01 covers ABB Ability Zenon — the SCADA/HMI platform used across energy, water and manufacturing — flagging an improper-serialization weakness in an embedded MongoDB authorization component that could be abused to affect access control. ICSA-26-218-02 covers the Johnson Controls TL280 communicator, where a flaw could let an attacker read sensitive information off the device; CISA lists impact across Critical Manufacturing, Commercial Facilities, Government Facilities, Transportation and Energy. Neither is reported as exploited, but Zenon sits at the supervisory layer of many plants and TL280-class communicators bridge building and life-safety systems to networks, so both warrant an inventory cross-check and CISA’s standard “keep it off the internet” hardening.

items.title: Water Cyber Shield Act introduced in the Senate, aiming roughly $300M a year at utility cyber defence
items.content_text: Senators Amy Klobuchar and Adam Schiff introduced the Water Cyber Shield Act of 2026 on 10 August, a direct response to the campaign against internet-exposed water-sector PLCs that hit more than 30 community systems in Minnesota alone (see top story). The bill would distribute on the order of $300 million a year to drinking-water and wastewater utilities for cybersecurity improvements, strengthen EPA oversight of sector cyber requirements, and expand technical assistance aimed at the small systems least able to fund a programme of their own. This is an introduced bill, not law — no obligation attaches to any utility today, and it must clear committee and both chambers first. It runs alongside the Senate EPW Committee’s bipartisan WRDA 2026, which would expressly extend water-resilience funding to reducing cybersecurity vulnerabilities and encourage WaterISAC participation. Plan on the assumption that money and expectations arrive together.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Sens. Klobuchar & Schiff bill introduction / Senate EPW WRDA 2026 — via The Record, UPI & Industrial Cyber

items.title: OT security coalition presses Congress and CISA for reforms and grants after the multi-state water hacks
items.content_text: With the water-utility campaign now spanning at least seven states (see top story), a coalition of OT-focused security firms went public on 3 August urging federal action rather than another round of voluntary guidance. Their asks are concrete: Congress should reauthorize and fully fund the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program — the main channel of money to the small, cash-strapped municipal utilities being hit — confirm Andrew McClure to lead the Department of Energy’s CESER office, and reauthorize the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 before its lapse chills threat-sharing. The through-line is that most affected water and wastewater operators lack the budget and staff to segment or monitor OT on their own, so the coalition wants durable funding and clearer federal authority behind CISA’s “get PLCs off the internet” message. For asset owners it signals where grant dollars and mandates may soon flow.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: OT security industry coalition statement — via Cybersecurity Dive & Nextgov/FCW

items.title: CISA and Five Eyes partners publish “CI Fortify” — pre-engineer OT isolation before an attack, not during one
items.content_text: On 28 July CISA, Australia’s ASD/ACSC, the UK NCSC, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security and the FBI released joint guidance, “CI Fortify — Advice for Isolating Vital Systems,” giving critical-infrastructure operators practical steps to cut vital OT and enabling systems off from all other networks during a crisis and keep delivering the essential service in isolation for an extended period. The core message is that isolation has to be identified, engineered and rehearsed in advance: first define the minimum systems needed to keep the service running, then document every connection those systems have to corporate networks, remote access, cloud, internet-facing infrastructure, vendors and other operators, and build tested separation points you can actually invoke. Landing the same week as the Minnesota water incident (see top story), it is the defensive counterpart to that scenario — a ready-made framework for the manual-fallback and disconnect decisions those utilities had to make live.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA / ASD’s ACSC / UK NCSC / CCCS / FBI joint guidance — via CISA & BleepingComputer

items.title: NERC opens comment on CIP-013-4 — supply-chain risk assessments would get mandatory reassessment clocks
items.content_text: Draft 1 of CIP-013-4, a proposed revision to NERC’s supply-chain risk-management standard, is out for formal comment and initial ballot. The draft widens applicability to associated EACMS, PACS, PCAs and Shared Cyber Infrastructure, and — the substantive change — adds defined reassessment timelines: utilities would have to re-run the supply-chain risk assessment before deploying a product or service whenever the most recent assessment is older than 24 months for high-impact systems or 36 months for medium-impact systems, explicitly including spare equipment and emergency repairs. It is the direction of travel on SCRM: periodic, evidenced reassessment rather than a one-time vendor review. Registered entities should read the draft now and model what rolling 24/36-month assessment cycles would mean for their procurement and spares processes.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: NERC CIP-013-4 Draft 1 (comment/initial ballot) — via Fortress Information Security compliance report

items.title: OT Cyber Coalition pushes to make ISA/IEC 62443 the single global OT standard
items.content_text: The Operational Technology Cybersecurity Coalition released a position paper on 23 July urging US policymakers to formally recognize ISA/IEC 62443 as the global baseline for OT cybersecurity, arguing that an expanding patchwork of sector-specific mandates piles on compliance cost without improving real security. The paper points to the TSA’s pipeline security directives, NERC CIP’s “double-reporting” burden in the energy sector, and the EU’s overlapping NIS2, CER and Cyber Resilience Act requirements as cases where fragmented rules re-create controls already defined in 62443. For asset owners it is a useful signal of where harmonization pressure is building — and a reminder that a 62443-anchored program tends to map cleanly onto most of these regimes at once.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: OT Cybersecurity Coalition position paper — via Industrial Cyber
